<div class="hero"><h2>Part II: make the localhost product portable and public</h2><p>Part I produced a working XGBoost model, Flask API and Streamlit UI. Now we package each service, reproduce it with Docker, push source to GitHub, and deploy the containers to Google Cloud Run.</p></div>

<a class="navbtn" href="model-deployment-part-1.html">← Part I: Data, XGBoost, Flask & Streamlit</a>
<a class="navbtn" href="model-deployment-part-3.html">Part III: Hosting alternatives →</a>

## 1. Where Part I ended

Part I saved the fitted pipeline at:

```text
artifacts/energy_xgb_pipeline.joblib
```

and Flask loaded it at startup with:

```python
MODEL = joblib.load(MODEL_PATH)
```

The Streamlit application did **not** load the model. It called Flask through HTTP. We preserve that architecture in production.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Streamlit container  ── HTTPS ──> Flask API container
                                      │
                                      ▼
                         energy_xgb_pipeline.joblib
```

## 2. Why Docker?

<div class="concept"><strong>Image vs container.</strong> A Docker <em>image</em> is an immutable recipe containing code, Python dependencies and startup instructions. A <em>container</em> is a running instance of that image. “It works on my laptop” becomes less important because development and cloud execute the same image.</div>

We will create **two images** because frontend and backend scale independently.

## 3. Backend Dockerfile

The backend image includes the serialized model because Flask must load it when the container starts. Create `Dockerfile.backend` in the project root.

```{.dockerfile filename="Dockerfile.backend"}
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY artifacts/ ./artifacts/
COPY backend/ ./backend/
ENV PORT=8080
CMD exec gunicorn --bind :${PORT} --workers 2 --threads 4 --timeout 120 backend.app:app
```

<div class="action"><strong>What happens at startup?</strong> Docker starts Gunicorn → Gunicorn imports <code>backend.app:app</code> → importing `backend/app.py` executes `joblib.load(...)` once per worker → the worker is ready to answer requests.</div>

### Why Gunicorn instead of `app.run()`?

Flask's development server is for development. Gunicorn is a production WSGI process manager: it can run multiple workers, handle signals correctly, and work naturally in container platforms.

## 4. Frontend Dockerfile

Create `Dockerfile.frontend`.

```{.dockerfile filename="Dockerfile.frontend"}
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY frontend/ ./frontend/
ENV PORT=8080
CMD streamlit run frontend/streamlit_app.py \
    --server.address=0.0.0.0 \
    --server.port=${PORT} \
    --server.headless=true
```

Notice that the frontend image does **not** copy `artifacts/`. It needs only the Flask URL.

## 5. `.dockerignore`

```{.text filename=".dockerignore"}
.git
.gitignore
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
venv/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
data/
artifacts/test_predictions.csv
```

Do not exclude `artifacts/energy_xgb_pipeline.joblib`; the backend image needs it.

## 6. Build and run locally

<div class="action"><strong>Action.</strong> Build two reproducible images, then run the backend on port 8000 and Streamlit on 8501.</div>

```{.bash}
docker build -f Dockerfile.backend -t energy-api:local .
docker build -f Dockerfile.frontend -t energy-ui:local .
```

Create a network and run both containers:

```{.bash}
docker network create energy-net

docker run --rm --name energy-api --network energy-net \
  -p 8000:8080 energy-api:local
```

In another terminal:

```{.bash}
docker run --rm --name energy-ui --network energy-net \
  -p 8501:8080 \
  -e API_BASE_URL=http://energy-api:8080 \
  energy-ui:local
```

Open `http://localhost:8501`.

<div class="result"><strong>Important networking idea.</strong> Inside Docker, `localhost` means “this same container.” Streamlit reaches Flask through Docker DNS name <code>energy-api</code>, not `localhost`.</div>

## 7. Docker Compose: one command for the complete product

Create `compose.yaml`.

```{.yaml filename="compose.yaml"}
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.backend
    ports:
      - "8000:8080"

  ui:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.frontend
    ports:
      - "8501:8080"
    environment:
      API_BASE_URL: http://api:8080
    depends_on:
      - api
```

Run:

```{.bash}
docker compose up --build
```

Stop:

```{.bash}
docker compose down
```

## 8. GitHub: source control, not the runtime

<div class="concept"><strong>Three different things.</strong> GitHub stores source history. A container registry stores built images. Cloud Run executes containers. Keeping these concepts separate makes cloud architecture much easier to understand.</div>

```text
GitHub repository ──build──> Container image ──store──> Artifact Registry
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                                 Cloud Run service
```

### GitHub credentials

For command-line pushes, use either GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`) or SSH. Do not put a GitHub password/token inside source files.

```{.bash}
git add .
git commit -m "Part II: Dockerize API and Streamlit"
git push origin main
```

## 9. Choose a production target: Google Cloud Run

<div class="action"><strong>Why Cloud Run for this course?</strong> It teaches the transferable container model: build an image, deploy a service, inject configuration, receive an HTTPS URL, and let the platform scale instances with traffic. It also avoids teaching students to administer a VM before they understand deployment.</div>

The architecture becomes:

```text
                    Internet
                       │
             ┌─────────▼─────────┐
             │ Streamlit Cloud Run│
             └─────────┬─────────┘
                       │ HTTPS + API_BASE_URL
             ┌─────────▼─────────┐
             │ Flask Cloud Run   │
             │ + XGBoost artifact│
             └───────────────────┘
```

## 10. Google Cloud prerequisites and credentials

You need a Google Cloud project with billing enabled and the `gcloud` CLI installed. Authenticate interactively on your own machine:

```{.bash}
gcloud auth login
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
```

<div class="warningbox"><strong>Credentials rule.</strong> Never paste downloaded service-account JSON keys into GitHub. For local learning, use interactive `gcloud auth login`. For automated CI/CD, prefer short-lived identity federation / platform-managed service accounts rather than long-lived keys.</div>

Enable the services used below:

```{.bash}
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com \
  cloudbuild.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com
```

Set shell variables:

```{.bash}
export PROJECT_ID="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
export REGION="us-central1"
export REPOSITORY="energy-ml"
```

## 11. Create an Artifact Registry repository

Artifact Registry stores container images.

```{.bash}
gcloud artifacts repositories create $REPOSITORY \
  --repository-format=docker \
  --location=$REGION \
  --description="MLStation energy deployment images"
```

## 12. Build the backend image in Google Cloud

Cloud Build reads our Dockerfile and pushes the resulting image into Artifact Registry.

```{.bash}
gcloud builds submit \
  --tag $REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/energy-api:v1 \
  --file Dockerfile.backend .
```

### Deploy Flask

```{.bash}
gcloud run deploy energy-api \
  --image $REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/energy-api:v1 \
  --region $REGION \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --port 8080 \
  --memory 1Gi \
  --cpu 1 \
  --min 0 \
  --max 10
```

Cloud Run prints an HTTPS service URL. Save it:

```{.bash}
export API_URL="https://YOUR-ENERGY-API-URL.run.app"
curl "$API_URL/health"
curl "$API_URL/api/v1/meta"
```

<div class="result"><strong>The backend is now public.</strong> The cloud container loads the same <code>energy_xgb_pipeline.joblib</code> that you tested locally. No training occurs on Cloud Run startup.</div>

## 13. Build and deploy Streamlit

Build the frontend image:

```{.bash}
gcloud builds submit \
  --tag $REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/energy-ui:v1 \
  --file Dockerfile.frontend .
```

Deploy it and inject the Flask URL as an environment variable:

```{.bash}
gcloud run deploy energy-ui \
  --image $REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/energy-ui:v1 \
  --region $REGION \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --port 8080 \
  --set-env-vars API_BASE_URL=$API_URL \
  --memory 1Gi \
  --cpu 1 \
  --min 0 \
  --max 10
```

Open the HTTPS URL returned for `energy-ui`.

## 14. What “scaling” means here

If one container instance can process roughly $\mu$ requests/second and traffic arrives at rate $\lambda$, utilization is conceptually related to

$$\rho=\frac{\lambda}{c\mu},$$

where $c$ is the number of active instances. Real autoscaling is more nuanced, but the intuition is useful: more concurrent demand eventually requires more serving capacity.

Cloud Run can add instances; `--max 10` protects against uncontrolled scaling/cost. `--min 0` permits scale-to-zero, trading some first-request latency for lower idle cost.

## 15. Production improvements

For a teaching project, public unauthenticated prediction is convenient. A serious system should additionally consider authentication, request-size limits, schema validation (for example Pydantic), rate limiting, structured logs, monitoring, model registry/versioning, drift monitoring, CI/CD, vulnerability scanning, and private service-to-service authentication.

## 16. End state

<div class="pipeline">
GitHub source → Docker build → Artifact Registry → Flask Cloud Run<br>
GitHub source → Docker build → Artifact Registry → Streamlit Cloud Run<br>
Browser → Streamlit HTTPS → Flask HTTPS → loaded XGBoost pipeline → prediction
</div>
